teaser: Four tons of basalt, carried off an island in 1868, and still asked for by the people who carved it.

lesson.text: About four tons. That is what this figure weighs, nearly as much as three family cars, and it is carved from a single block of basalt, a dark volcanic rock so hard that steel tools struggle with it. Its makers had no metal at all. They had other stones.

He comes from Rapa Nui, the island outsiders call Easter Island, a speck of land in the Pacific more than 2,000 miles from the coast of Chile. Statues like him are called moai. Close to a thousand of them were carved there, most between about 1100 and 1600.

Almost all moai were cut from tuff, a soft rock made of compressed volcanic ash that can be shaped fairly quickly. Only a small handful are basalt like this one, which is one reason its edges are still so crisp after centuries.

A moai is not a portrait in our sense. It stands for an ancestor, a dead chief whose power still protects the living. So the carvers did not chase a likeness. They repeated a formula, and the formula is all in the head, which takes up about a third of the whole figure.

lesson.title: The formula
lesson.text: Three features make a moai a moai. Follow them from top to bottom.

spots.title: A cliff of a brow
spots.text: One heavy ridge runs straight across the forehead. Under it the eyes are just deep hollows, so the ceiling lights of the gallery fill them with shadow.

spots.title: Nose and lips
spots.text: The nose is long and flares at the nostrils. Just below, the thin lips push forward in a tight pout. Nothing here moves: the face is closed, proud, a little stern.

spots.title: A long ear
spots.text: The ear is stretched into a tall, narrow slab against the side of the head. Long ears are a constant of moai carving.

lesson.text: Those hollow eyes were not always meant to stay empty. On some moai set up on ceremonial platforms, archaeologists have found eyes of white coral with dark stone pupils, slotted in for rituals. With eyes, the ancestor was awake.

Below the jaw the carving becomes almost shy. The body is a smooth column with only a few marks on it: two small raised nipples, thin arms pressed flat against the sides, and one more line that is easy to miss.
The sculptor gave this giant a collarbone: a single thin line that dips to a point. Can you spot it?

spots.title: The collarbone
spots.text: Right under the chin, a fine raised line curves across the chest and dips into a small V at the center. One stroke is enough to tell you where the neck ends and the body starts.

lesson.text: A moai says a lot with very little. A huge head, a ridge for a brow, a line for a collarbone: the body is reduced to signs, and that economy is what makes it feel so powerful.

What this photo cannot show you is his back. It is covered in later carvings: two figures with human bodies and bird heads facing each other, a small bird, and ceremonial paddles. They belong to the birdman religion that took over on the island after the age of the great statues.

Each spring, champions from rival clans swam through rough water to a rocky islet and waited for the first egg of a seabird, the sooty tern. The patron of the man who brought it back became the sacred “birdman” for a year.

In 1868 the crew of a British warship, HMS Topaze, found the statue half buried inside a stone house at the ceremonial village of Orongo. They dug it out, dragged it to the shore and floated it to the ship. The crew reported that it was painted red and white, and that the color washed away in the sea.

The ship reached England in 1869. Queen Victoria was offered the statue and passed it on to the British Museum, where it has stood ever since, 2.42 meters (about 8 feet) of dark stone under spotlights, with visitors walking around its base as you see here.
The name Hoa Hakananai'a was recorded by the sailors who took him away. It is usually translated as “stolen friend” or “lost friend.”

In 2018 a delegation from Rapa Nui traveled to London to ask for him back. For the islanders he is not an artwork but an ancestor, a living presence. The museum has talked about a loan. The question of where he belongs is still open.

quiz.question: What is unusual about the stone of this moai?
options: It is basalt, while most moai are soft tuff
It is marble brought from Chile
It is coral from the reef
quiz.explanation: Only a handful of moai are carved in hard basalt.

quiz.question: What does a moai represent?
options: An ancestor whose power protects the living
quiz.explanation: Moai stand for dead chiefs who still watch over the community.

quiz.question: What filled the eye hollows of some moai during rituals?
options: White coral with dark stone pupils
quiz.explanation: Archaeologists have found coral eyes made to slot into the sockets.

quiz.question: What is carved on the statue's back?
quiz.explanation: The back carries later carvings linked to the birdman religion.

quiz.question: How did the statue reach London?
options: It was bought at auction in 1920
It was taken by the crew of HMS Topaze in 1868
It was a gift from Chile
quiz.explanation: British sailors removed it from Orongo in 1868.

facts.text: The carvers of this moai worked with iron chisels.
facts.explanation: Rapa Nui had no metal: the statue was shaped with stone tools.

facts.text: The head takes up about a third of the whole figure.
facts.explanation: The moai formula puts nearly everything into the head.

facts.text: The name Hoa Hakananai'a is usually translated as “stolen friend” or “lost friend.”
facts.explanation: That is the name recorded when the statue was taken away.
